key_insight: Machine-learned long-time simulations reveal that small polarons at oxygen-deficient rutile TiO2(110) surfaces move far more slowly than in bulk because surface hopping pathways are restricted.
engineering_relevance: This explains why porous rutile TiO2 can show lower electron mobility than single-crystal material and helps guide surface engineering for catalysis and energy devices.
method: Extended machine-learning-assisted polaron dynamics to a reducible oxide surface
Ran several nanoseconds of finite-temperature dynamics on oxygen-deficient rutile TiO2(110)
Compared surface vs bulk polaron hopping pathways and mobility
evidence_signal: The study uses nanosecond-scale simulations across multiple temperatures to quantify hopping statistics and show orders-of-magnitude mobility suppression at the reduced surface.
watch_item: The approach relies on a trained machine-learning model, so transferability and accuracy should be checked carefully for other oxide surfaces or defect chemistries.
paper_title: Machine-learned dynamics of surface polarons at reduced oxide surfaces
